chapters.title: Chapter 5: Agri Commodities and Base Metals

lessons.title: Why Agri Contracts Get Suspended: SEBI Curbs, Price Limits and Delivery Risk

children.text: On 20 December 2021, soybean processors, mustard oil millers and traders across Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Gujarat learned that seven of India's most important agri futures contracts would effectively stop. SEBI directed the exchanges not to launch new contracts in paddy (non-basmati), wheat, chana, mustard seed, soybean, crude palm oil and moong, and to allow only the squaring off of existing positions. Initially meant to last a year, the suspension was extended again and again. No gold or crude oil trader has ever faced anything like it. By the end of this lesson you will understand why agri contracts get suspended, how daily price limits can trap you in a position, and the delivery risks that make agri futures fundamentally different from the rest of the commodity market.

body.text: In agri futures, policy risk sits on top of price risk. Food prices are politically sensitive, so exchanges and regulators can limit, halt or suspend trading, and a trader must plan for the market itself becoming unavailable.

body.text: Suspensions and extensions are announced through SEBI orders and exchange circulars, sometimes with very little notice. The list of suspended contracts can change. Always check the latest SEBI and exchange circulars before planning a position or a hedge in any agri commodity.

children.text: Why Regulators Suspend Agri Contracts

The recurring reason is food inflation. When prices of staples like wheat, pulses or edible oil rise sharply, futures markets are often accused of fuelling speculation, because futures prices move first and visibly.

body.title: The debate over agri futures suspensions

columns.label: The case made for suspension
points: Futures may attract speculative money that amplifies price rises in essential foods
Visible futures prices can influence expectations and hoarding in physical markets
Temporarily removing the market can calm sentiment during an inflation spike
Government stock limits and export curbs may conflict with open futures positions

columns.label: The case made against suspension
points: Futures mostly reflect supply shortages rather than cause them; shooting the messenger does not add supply
Farmers, FPOs and processors lose their main tool for hedging price risk
Price discovery moves to opaque physical and informal markets
Repeated suspensions damage confidence, liquidity and participation for years

body.label: The evidence question
body.context: After futures in several agri commodities were suspended in 2007 and 2008, a government-appointed expert committee led by economist Abhijit Sen studied whether futures trading drove food inflation. It did not find conclusive evidence that futures trading had caused the price rises.

body.title: What can you still do?
body.question: Under a suspension like SEBI's December 2021 order, what could a trader who already held a position in a suspended contract do?
options: Add to the position at a discount
Only square off, meaning close, the existing position
Roll the position into the next month's contract
Nothing, because all positions were cancelled at zero
body.explanation: The order stopped new contracts and new positions. Existing positions could be squared off. Rolling was not possible, because it requires opening a position in a new contract.

children.text: Daily Price Limits: When the Market Stops Moving

markDefs.definition: The maximum amount, usually a percentage of the previous day's settlement price, that a futures contract is allowed to rise or fall in one trading day. Exchanges can relax it in stages after a cooling-off period.

children.text: Even when a contract is trading normally, exchanges cap how far its price can move in a single day. This is the
daily price limit
(DPL). It is usually set as a percentage of the previous day's settlement price, and exchanges can relax it in stages after a cooling-off period when the limit is hit.

body.latex: \text{Upper limit} = S_{\text{prev}} \times (1 + L) \qquad \text{Lower limit} = S_{\text{prev}} \times (1 - L)
body.caption: S_prev is the previous day's settlement price and L is the applicable daily price limit. Actual limits differ by contract; check the exchange specification.

body.title: Find the upper limit
body.prompt: An NCDEX contract settled yesterday at ₹24,000 per quintal. Its daily price limit is 4%. What is today's upper price limit, in rupees per quintal?
body.explanation: ₹24,000 × 1.04 = ₹24,960. The lower limit would be ₹24,000 × 0.96 = ₹23,040. No trades can take place outside this band unless the exchange relaxes the limit.

children.text: The Trap of a Locked Limit

markDefs.definition: A situation where the price reaches the daily price limit and stays there with orders only on one side, so traders who want to exit cannot find a counterparty.

children.text: Price limits are meant to slow panic. But when the news is bad enough, buyers disappear and the price sits at the lower limit with sellers stacked up and nobody willing to buy. The contract is then
locked at the limit
. If you are on the wrong side, you cannot get out, and the next day the limit resets lower.

body.title: Illustrative agri contract hitting its 4% lower limit on consecutive days (₹ per quintal)

children.text: Day 1:
bad news breaks. The price falls from ₹5,000 to the 4% lower limit of ₹4,800 and closes there.
Day 2:
it opens near the new lower limit of ₹4,608 (4% below ₹4,800) and quickly locks there, with almost no buyers.
Day 3:
it opens at the next limit, ₹4,424, before finally finding buyers and bouncing.

body.title: Why a stop-loss did not save the long trader

children.text: Suppose a trader was long a position of 100 quintals at ₹5,000 with a stop-loss at ₹4,850, a planned loss of ₹15,000.
Day 1: the price blew through ₹4,850 on the way to the limit. With heavy selling, the order may execute only at or near ₹4,800, a loss of ₹20,000.
If the order did not execute on Day 1, on Day 2 it could not execute at all while the price was locked at ₹4,608 with no buyers.
A trader finally exiting on Day 3 at ₹4,430 would lose (₹5,000 minus ₹4,430) × 100 = ₹57,000, nearly four times the planned loss.
Price limits protect the system from disorderly moves, but they can turn an ordinary stop-loss into a much larger loss for an individual trader.

body.title: Name the trap
body.textWithBlank: When a futures price reaches its daily price limit and stays there with no buyers, traders say the contract is ___ at the limit.
body.explanation: A locked limit means orders exist on only one side. Traders on the wrong side cannot exit until the price moves off the limit, often at a much worse level the next day.

children.text: Extra Margins and Position Limits
Before reaching for suspensions, exchanges and SEBI usually use gentler tools to cool an overheated agri contract.
Additional or special margins.
Exchanges can impose extra margins on long or short positions, or both, sometimes overnight. Traders who cannot fund them must reduce positions.
Position limits.
Caps on how large a position any single client or broker can hold, often tighter for near-month contracts, to stop any one participant from cornering supply.
Tighter price limits.
Narrower daily limits during volatile periods.
No new contracts.
Exchanges can stop launching far-month contracts, gradually shrinking the market.

body.text: Watch for these gentler measures as early warnings. A sequence of special margins, tighter limits and position curbs in an agri contract often precedes stronger regulatory action. When you see them stack up, reduce size or step aside.

children.text: Delivery Risk: The Physical Reality of Agri Futures
Most NCDEX agri contracts settle by physical delivery. That brings risks a gold ETF investor never faces.

body.caption: Key delivery risks in agri futures

cells: Open positions at expiry must be settled by giving or taking delivery, with no choice to settle in cash
Speculators who forget to close before the delivery period
Produce that fails assaying at the accredited warehouse is rejected or accepted at a discount
Delivery happens at specific centres; moving goods there, or taking them away, costs money and time
Both buyers and sellers far from the delivery centre
Agri produce can lose quality or weight over time; warehouse charges add up
Buyers who take delivery and hold stock
The final price may be based on spot prices polled at the delivery centre, which can diverge from recent futures trading
Sellers who fail to deliver face penalties

body.text: An agri futures position held into the delivery period is no longer just a price bet. A long speculator can end up paying for tonnes of produce in a warehouse hundreds of kilometres away, with quality, storage and resale all now their problem. For most retail traders, the rule is simple: close or roll well before the delivery period begins.

body.title: An FPO without a hedge
body.scenario: The Sehore Kisan Producer Company, a farmer producer organisation in Madhya Pradesh with 1,200 member farmers, used to sell soybean futures on NCDEX at sowing time to lock in prices for part of the expected harvest. Since the December 2021 suspension, it cannot do this. The CEO asks: "How else can we protect our farmers from a price crash at harvest?"
body.prompt: What alternatives could the FPO consider, and what are their limitations?
body.modelAnswer:
Possible alternatives:
1. Forward contracts with processors. The FPO can agree prices and quantities directly with soybean processors or feed makers before harvest. Limitation: these carry counterparty risk and are hard to enforce if prices move sharply.
2. MSP procurement. Soybean has a minimum support price. Limitation: government procurement may be limited in scale and location, and MSP is only a floor, not a fixed selling price.
3. Storage and warehouse receipt finance. Instead of selling at harvest lows, the FPO can store in accredited warehouses and borrow against electronic warehouse receipts, selling later when arrivals ease. Limitation: storage and interest costs, and prices may not recover.
4. Staggered selling. Selling portions over several months spreads price risk. Limitation: it reduces, but does not remove, exposure.
5. Related contracts, if available. Hedging with a correlated commodity that is still trading introduces basis risk and may not track soybean closely.

The broader lesson: the FPO's price risk did not disappear when the futures market was suspended. It simply lost its most efficient, transparent tool to manage that risk.

body.title: Before trading any agri futures contract
steps: Check the latest SEBI and exchange circulars for suspensions, special margins or restrictions on that commodity.
Note the daily price limit and how and when it can be relaxed.
Check position limits, especially for the near-month contract.
Confirm whether the contract is compulsory delivery, and when the delivery or tender period begins.
Check volume and open interest so you know you can exit.
Size the position assuming you might be locked at the limit for more than one day.

body.label: SEBI: Circulars and orders
body.description: Search SEBI's circulars and orders for current directions on commodity derivatives, including suspensions and their extensions.

cards.definition: SEBI halted new trading in paddy (non-basmati), wheat, chana, mustard seed, soybean, crude palm oil and moong.
A restriction allowing traders to close existing positions but not open new ones.
A 2008 expert committee that did not find conclusive evidence that futures trading caused food inflation.
The maximum one-day price move allowed, as a percentage of the previous settlement price.
Price stuck at the daily limit with no counterparties, preventing exits.
Extra margin imposed by an exchange on volatile contracts, often at short notice.
Settlement where open positions at expiry must give or take physical delivery.
Refusal of delivered produce that fails the contract's quality specification.

points: Agri futures carry policy risk: SEBI suspended new trading in seven key agri commodities in December 2021 and extended the suspension repeatedly.
Suspensions usually follow food inflation concerns, though expert reviews such as the Abhijit Sen Committee did not find conclusive evidence that futures caused price rises.
Suspensions remove hedging tools from farmers, FPOs and processors, pushing price risk back onto them.
Daily price limits can lock a contract at the limit, making stop-losses ineffective and losses larger than planned.
Special margins, position limits and tighter price bands are early warning signs of stronger action.
Most agri contracts settle by compulsory physical delivery, with quality, location and storage risks, so speculators should exit well before delivery periods.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or legal advice. The status of suspended contracts, price limits and margin rules changes over time; always check current SEBI and exchange circulars. Price examples are illustrative. Commodity derivatives are leveraged and can cause losses larger than your initial margin.
